$comment: Mutation gate. Each entry deletes one safety control and names the tests that
must go red as a result. A control nothing notices the removal of is either
decorative or untested, and both are worth knowing.
Why this exists as a gate rather than an exercise: this repository's recurring
defect is a check that reports success without having run — an assertion behind
a swallowed TypeError, a test whose guard skipped it, a mutation whose search
string the shell expanded to nothing. Coverage cannot see any of them. Killing
Adding a control here is cheap and the right instinct. `find` must appear
exactly once in the file, so a mutant cannot silently stop applying — the
failure mode that made one of these look like it survived when it had never
A mutant that is expected to hang rather than fail may set `timeoutSeconds`
to override the runner's default budget for its run.
See README.md for the runner's own guards and why hangs count as kills.

mutants.control: An existing directory with no valid receipt view is refused, so files Anvil did not write are never deleted.
A different vendor/gateway/API/environment lineage may never replace an existing bundle directory.
Rollback restores the previous bundle whole, so an interrupted install leaves one complete bundle or the other.
Output deliberately changed after import is not discarded without --replace-derived.
Derived state is verified against the exact digest recorded at approval before it is discarded.
A stale manifest naming files that are neither compiler output nor recognized lifecycle state cannot authorise deleting them.
A preserved lifecycle artifact may not silently overwrite a compiler-owned candidate file.
Attesting a supplied contract over a gateway definition is defined only for WSO2 native lineage.
The recorded public gateway coordinate must be HTTPS.
A gateway URL carrying embedded credentials is refused before it reaches a receipt.
'unscoped' is reserved for lineage whose gateway identity was never proven and cannot be supplied as a real one.
--strict-identity requires an explicit gateway id, because an offline export cannot prove its own control-plane identity.
An override recorded when the digests already match would be a false claim in the receipt, so it is refused.
A locked entrypoint absent from its own source manifest establishes no lineage.
Anvil will not infer which of several embedded definitions is authoritative; route compatibility is not byte lineage.
An operator's runtime-coordinate attestation supersedes the missing-coordinate warning rather than sitting beside it.
Path parameters are positional, so /t/{id} and /t/{thingId} are the same route; without this the route-set attestation reports false differences.
A non-regular filesystem node is refused before it is read. readFileSync on a FIFO blocks forever, so this is a liveness boundary as much as a correctness one.
mutants.$timeout: This mutant does not fail, it hangs, so the runner's timeout is what kills it. 45s rather than the 180s default: the honest run of this set takes ~11s on a CI runner, so 45s is 4x headroom against contention while keeping the one deliberate hang from dominating the gate's wall clock (it was 3m01s of a 4m09s run).

mutants.control: A generated SDK refuses a confirmation-gated operation locally, before anything reaches the wire.
A generated SDK refuses a mutation whose contract requires an idempotency key Anvil cannot derive.
Certification refuses an SDK manifest whose confirmation, human-approval, idempotency, or retry flags differ from AIR.
The observed-reality lane drives reads only; a mutation is never sent to a customer's running system, whatever the config lists.
A read may only claim that an operation the application does not serve is gone; recorded traffic's high reliability must not launder a claim the observation never earned.
A Postman request dropped because its (path, method) is already taken is reported, never lost silently.
An adopted MCP tool without a readOnlyHint is a non-idempotent mutation that confirms — unknown side effect beats assumed safety.

The runtime refuses an operation whose wire protocol it cannot speak. Without it a SOAP/GraphQL/gRPC operation is posted as JSON to a coordinate Anvil invented — a well-formed lie, indistinguishable on the wire from a real request.
mutants.find:
if (verdict.ok) return undefined;
  // A facade declares that the base URL serves the synthesized *coordinates*
mutants.replace:
if (true) return undefined;
  // A facade declares that the base URL serves the synthesized *coordinates*

mutants.control: Each non-REST source kind maps to the protocol it actually speaks. Collapsing wsdl to http_json is exactly the conflation this module exists to end: a source format is not a wire protocol.

Certification refuses a bundle whose wire protocol the runtime cannot speak. Without it a SOAP bundle with servers: [] certifies with zero failures, because every hermetic lane compares the bundle against a mock generated from the same AIR.
The compiler says at compile time what the runtime and certification will refuse later, so an unexecutable transport is not first heard about at deploy.
mutants.replace: const wire = { ok: true } as ReturnType<typeof wireExecutability>;

mutants.control: The endpoint a WSDL declares in <soap:address> reaches AIR. Dropping it made service.servers empty and the generated skill state, falsely, that the source declares no server URL.

The generated clients refuse an operation whose wire protocol they cannot speak. The SDKs do not go through the runtime's executor, so a gate that lived only there would leave four surfaces free to send the lie.
Certification checks the SDK manifest's declared wire protocol against AIR, so a client that believes it speaks HTTP+JSON to a SOAP operation is caught rather than shipped.

A credential carried in the endpoint's query string never reaches the snapshot, the AIR, or anything derived from them. An MCP endpoint's token lives there by convention (Moodle's ?wstoken=), and these artifacts are written to disk and echoed by --json.

A document that compiles to no operations is not the application's contract. Accepting one turns an auth wall or a wrong path into a successful acquisition whose diff reports every operation as removed — a wall of false blocking drift that reads like a real emergency.

A probeReads id this bundle does not define fails the lane. Dropping it silently is how a typo, or an operation renamed out of the bundle, quietly stops covering the endpoint it was added for while CI keeps going green.
A probe that answered with an error fails the lane. The operation was asked and nothing was learned about whether the compiled model matches the application, which is not the same as agreement.
A contract endpoint that was configured but could not be read fails the lane. Not asking is a legitimate posture; asking and getting no answer is a question the operator believes was answered.
The envelope's body element carries the namespace the WSDL declares. An unqualified element is the single commonest reason a real SOAP server rejects an otherwise correct request.
SOAP 1.1 sends the action as its own quoted header; a 1.1 server dispatches on it and answers a missing one with a fault.

A soap:Fault is refused rather than returned as a result. Servers deliver one with HTTP 200 as readily as 500, so the status is not the answer — and reporting one as success would record a failed mutation in the idempotency ledger as completed.
mutants.find: const fault = codec && isFaultAware(codec) ? codec.faultIn(op, res) : undefined;

mutants.control: Only a transport-layer Server fault is transient. An application fault — a rejected transfer, an unknown account — fails identically on retry, and retrying a mutation on one is exactly what the safety contract forbids.

Only document/literal is claimed. An rpc binding wraps the parts in an operation-named element and encoded carries per-element type attributes; neither is implemented, so the compiler records no binding and the transport gate keeps refusing rather than the codec encoding on a guess.

The XML reader refuses DOCTYPE and ENTITY declarations. A DTD is the prerequisite for both external-entity expansion (XXE) and the billion-laughs denial of service; refusing it makes both unparseable rather than defended against.

Certification compares each generated client's declared SOAPAction against AIR. A client that dispatches on the wrong action is refused by the service; one that sends none is refused by a 1.1 server outright.
use="encoded" carries per-element type attributes Anvil does not emit. Refused rather than encoded on a guess.
A message described by type rather than element gives the envelope no body element QName to qualify. Refused rather than invented.

Every argument becomes a declared GraphQL variable, so no caller value is ever interpolated into query text. A value spliced into a statement is a value that can rewrite the statement — the same rule the SQL query policy enforces one layer over.

GraphQL reports failures inside a 200 with an errors array. Reported as a result, a failed mutation would be recorded in the idempotency ledger as completed — and a partial response is still a failure, since AIR's output contract describes one shape.
Certification compares each generated client's query document against AIR. A client posting a different document is asking a different question.
A streaming RPC records no binding. A stream is not a request and a response, and no JSON transcoder turns one into a single exchange.

gRPC is refused until an operator declares a transcoder. Its path is real, which makes the temptation to just call it strong — and a native gRPC server rejects JSON over HTTP/1.1, so calling it anyway is the original bug.

A path template whose pattern spans more than one path segment is refused. The runtime percent-encodes a path parameter, so a slash-bearing value would address a DIFFERENT resource and succeed against it — the worst shape of failure, since nothing errors.

Only a rule the proto DECLARED earns http_json. `json_transcoded` is a guess about a deployment the proto cannot see, and treating it as executable would post JSON at a native gRPC server that rejects it.

An annotated method whose rule Anvil declines records NO binding. Falling back to gRPC's own coordinate would aim the call at a path the gateway provably does not serve, since a gateway serves the declared route and no other.
A streaming RPC is refused before its annotation is read. No gateway turns a stream into one bounded request and response, so a declared route on one is not a route Anvil can take.
Two RPCs may declare different verbs on one route (GET and DELETE on /v1/items/{item_id}). Replacing the path entry instead of merging into it silently drops an approved operation from every surface.

An OData v2 FunctionImport that declares no m:HttpMethod is treated as a mutation. Defaulting it to GET would expose a write as a safe, auto-retryable read — the exact direction the asymmetric-trust rule forbids guessing in.
A multi-file Swagger 2.0 reference Anvil could not resolve fails the compile. Continuing would ship a surface smaller than the source describes, with no signal that anything was dropped.

The event bound is applied to the bytes that leave the transport, not only to the loop condition. A burst delivers hundreds of events in ONE socket read, so by the time the counter is re-checked the buffer already holds them all — this is the bug that reached a live run.

Only a frame carrying `data:` counts toward the event bound. A server holding an idle subscription open sends comment frames, and counting those lets a silent service exhaust a hundred-event window having published nothing at all.
mutants.replace: out.push({ end: match.index + match[0].length, isEvent: true });

mutants.control: A stream's own window is its deadline; the request timeout is only the backstop behind it. Left at the ordinary value the abort fires first, turning a subscription that legitimately saw nothing into a timeout — and then retrying it, because a read is retry-safe.

A frame Anvil never saw the end of is not reported, and that must depend on the missing boundary rather than on its JSON failing to parse — a frame cut just after its closing brace parses perfectly and is still an event that was never completed.

A subscription binding alone earns nothing: without a stream contract there is no bound, nothing makes the window close, and a call that never returns is not a call. This is what certification checks before a bundle is deployed.

A protocol facade declares coordinates, not framing. If it re-routed a subscription through the JSON codec, the call would lose `accept: text/event-stream` and its stream bound, and answer with one object where every other configuration answers with an array — one operation, two meanings, selected by an environment variable. `protocolFacadeApplies` extends the same refusal to every framing case (a streaming RPC, an rpc/encoded SOAP binding), so dropping it re-opens the hole for all of them.

The observation window's ceilings live on AIR's schema, so neither a manifest nor a hand-edited air.json can represent an unbounded window. Delete the ceiling and a five-minute cap becomes a connection held open as long as anyone asks.

Recorded traffic's one patch-bearing claim is deprecation, and only when NO observed call succeeded. Delete the check and an operation with live successes beside stale 404s gets proposed as deprecated — high-reliability evidence laundering a wrong conclusion.

Digests prove the bytes are the builder's bytes; the certification says whether those bytes ever passed the gates. Delete the gate and an uncertified or failed-certification pack installs silently — distribution without the trust that makes it safe to distribute.

Real model CLIs fence their JSON. Demanding that stdout parse whole scored 0/20 against a model that had in fact routed every task correctly — a measurement that silently reports failure for answers it was given is worse than no measurement, because a benchmark is believed.

An intent example sharing no word with its own operation's names teaches the skill to route by a vocabulary the MCP tool name does not have. Delete the corroboration filter and Anvil ships two surfaces that disagree about what an operation is called — the one failure this compiler exists to prevent.

Only a workflow that will actually register as a composite tool may supersede operation tools. Delete the gate and a SKIPPED workflow — unapproved, an unapproved step, a malformed binding, a later step demanding the caller's one idempotency key — silently deletes its members from tools/list and registers nothing in their place. The agent loses the operations and the thing that was supposed to stand in for them.

Async-status refusals must iterate to a fixed point against the evolving suppression set. Collapse the loop to one round and a chain — A serves and polls B, B polls C, both B and C proposed for suppression — ends with B refused (kept) but C still suppressed: the served surface lists B whose anvil/async_status_tool names a tool absent from tools/list, the exact half-contract the refusal exists to prevent.

A ubiquitous operation never becomes a grouping member. An operation present in nearly every distinct trace shape (auth, health check, token refresh) co-occurs with everything, so without this pre-filter it joins every grouping and the observed tasks collapse into one undifferentiated blob — the behavioural form of the FLEXCUBE /fcubsWarningResp candidate that was 64% of every candidate member in that report.

A trace shape seen a handful of times is an anecdote, not evidence. Delete the floor and every one-off session becomes a proposed capability, which is exactly the unfalsifiable taxonomy this lane exists to avoid producing.

The bare-CRUD-verb re-homing rule must never claim a verb word the estate itself uses as a real collection (a non-terminal path segment). Delete the guard and an estate with /count/{id}/lines loses its `count` resource to the rule — the exact over-reach the estate-wide pre-filter exists to prevent. It fired zero times on all six measured estates; that makes it insurance, and untested insurance is decoration.

The collision resolver must not append a distinguishing token the operation's canonicalName already ends with (compared singularized) — that is the tool-name stutter (`…_count_activities_activities`) an agent has to read past. Neutralize the check and the resolver reverts to appending the shortest token unconditionally.

The naming-conformance ratchet fails on ANY counter growth. Delete the comparison and a new semantic contradiction — a resource its own name text denies, a stuttering tool name — rides through the corpus lanes green, which is exactly how six naming defects sat unnoticed for months before the naming audit found them by hand.

The routing-accuracy ratchet fails when an estate's routing accuracy drops beyond the tolerance since the pinned baseline. Neutralize the comparison (always true) and a real routing regression — a task that used to route correctly and now does not — rides through the nightly refine-loop job green, exactly the failure mode the naming-conformance ratchet above already guards for a different signal.

An ambiguous path grammar never silently selects a grammar: when the estate's RPC and REST signals BOTH commit, the classifier must return `ambiguous` with a diagnostic naming both candidate grammars and fall back to the source kind's pre-classifier behavior — never let whichever side carries more votes win quietly. Delete the split-vote branch and a GET-heavy verb-terminal estate silently classifies rpc_plain with no warning.
A harness proposal naming a routing resource absent from the operation's own path and name vocabulary is refused by the resource_grounded_in_contract check.

An authored intent or routing phrase that the benchmark's own deterministic router sends to a DIFFERENT operation or capability than the one it was written for is not an example, it is a trap — refused by intent_routes_to_own_tool. Delete the refusal and a phrase like "list the views" (findings-log.md's helpdesk-views live loop) silently ships teaching an agent to route to the wrong tool, on a skill approval.ts auto-approves without a human ever seeing it.
A routing hub's edges never enter confusion-cluster construction, so one catalog-scale sink cannot weld unrelated confusable families into a single blob.

An authored capability is never born approved: a manifest `capabilities` entry with an `operations` list lands in AIR at lifecycle `proposed`, and can only reach `approved` through the same review gate (and disclosure budget) as a discovered grouping. Set the birth lifecycle to `approved` and a manifest author has silently skipped review — the exact shortcut the propose-only boundary exists to forbid.

A group proposal whose measured routing delta is NEGATIVE is refused with the numbers before it can reach review. Disable the comparison and a composition that measurably mangles routing sails to a reviewer wearing a benchmark-scored evidence claim — the admission gate reporting success without having gated.

Every non-GET request must carry the per-process token as X-Anvil-Console-Token, verbatim, or it is refused 403 before the body is read. Delete the check and any page open in the reviewer's browser can drive an approval through the console with a plain fetch.

Every non-GET request must carry an Origin equal to the server's own origin, or it is refused 403. Delete the check and a token that leaked once (a shared screenshot, a pasted page source) is enough for any other origin to mutate approval state.
A Sec-Fetch-Site the browser stamps as cross-site or same-site is refused even when the Origin header matches, so a request the browser itself says came from elsewhere never reaches a mutation.
mutants.find: if (site !== undefined && site !== "same-origin" && site !== "none") throw forbidden();

mutants.control: Every path a request body names (task, submission, pack out dir, receipt files, repository root) must resolve inside the workspace root, lexically and through symlinks, or it is refused 400 console/path_outside_root. Delete the check and the console reads and writes anywhere the reviewer's account can.

A bulk policy selects only rows the barrier lets through: non-idempotent, destructive, irreversible, confirmation-gated, and blocked operations, over-budget capabilities, and pack refinements without a positive measured delta are barred BEFORE any policy predicate runs, so a policy can only narrow the set, never widen it. Delete the barrier and a policy whose predicate says "everything" bulk-approves a non-idempotent financial mutation from the console.

A staged route's second hop is scored against ONLY the lane stage 1 entered, never the whole catalog — a real staged server has every other lane's tools closed, so a task whose target sits in a different lane must fail rather than pass through cross-lane leakage.
mutants.find: const stage2Outcome = await routeAndScore(router, intent, members, operationId);
mutants.replace: const stage2Outcome = await routeAndScore(router, intent, [...ladder.stage2.values()].flat(), operationId);

mutants.control: `anvil benchmark` with no --catalog flag stays flat: the default is decided in exactly one place, so the report it writes with no flag at all cannot silently gain the additive catalogs field or change what --check gates on.

An entry card folds at most MEMBER_INTENT_EXAMPLE_LIMIT of its member operations' own authored intent examples. The served card description is never truncated to the token budget (only the plan's own token accounting is, via entryCardTokens' Math.min), so this cap is the only thing keeping a lane with many verbose member intents from growing its actual served text unboundedly.

`auto` mode must refuse to ladder when a measured laddered-minus-flat accuracy delta falls below MIN_LADDERED_ACCURACY_DELTA_PTS. Weakening the floor would let `auto` serve a ladder measured to route meaningfully worse than the flat surface it replaces, with nothing telling the operator why.

A group workflow's supersedes may only name the proposal's own steps, and the named group_supersedes_within_steps check owns that refusal (the AIR schema's refinement is defense in depth behind it, not a substitute for the named rejection a harness is told to fix).

The OpenAI require_approval tier for a confirmation-required (or human-approval-gated) operation is always "always", never "never" — this is the one place that mapping is decided, and every openai target profile validation/generation call goes through it. Delete the mapping and a confirmation-required, irreversible-financial refund tool would be handed to the platform as require_approval: never.

`anvil certify` runs the target-kit-exact drift check for every registered profile whose subtree is present in the bundle, not only gemini-enterprise — the same regeneration proof Gemini always got. Narrow the loop back to one profile and a hand-tampered Claude, OpenAI, or MCP registry kit certifies clean.

`anvil status` regenerates and byte-compares the complete target subtree (verifyTargetKit) for any registered profile, not only gemini-enterprise; every other profile falls back to a shallow surfaceSignatureDigest-only freshness check that a tampered non-setup.json file never touches. Restrict the full check back to gemini-enterprise and a hand-edited Claude/OpenAI/MCP-registry kit file reports "fresh" with no findings.
A custom_header auth scheme resolves a carrier with no Bearer/Basic scheme prefix — the header (or query) value the SDKs send travels exactly as AIR declared, never disguised as a bearer token.
Generated SDK source never carries a literal PEM block — only the environment-variable NAME that reads it at runtime, even in a doc comment.
mutants.find: // material is never logged, echoed, or included in an error.

mutants.control: Every operation compiled from a HAR (captured-traffic) source is capped at review_required, never generated or approved — a capture is evidence of what happened once, never a declared contract. Delete the cap and a HAR-sourced operation compiles straight to generated, one anvil approve away from exposure with no human ever reviewing what the adapter templated or inferred.

A HAR capture's Cookie, Set-Cookie, Proxy-Authorization, and any header/query name matching /token|secret|key|password|session/i has its VALUE dropped before anything else in the adapter runs — only the carrier's NAME survives. Delete the drop and the original header (value intact) flows straight into the auth-scheme scan and the compiled document, leaking the real credential (an API key, a session cookie) into AIR the moment a HAR capture is compiled.

STOMP content-length is a byte count (encodeStompFrame emits Buffer.byteLength(body, "utf8")), and the parser must locate the body's NUL terminator by that same byte offset into the raw Buffer. Reintroduce string-length arithmetic — decoding to a string and walking UTF-16 code units instead of bytes — and any reply whose body contains a multibyte UTF-8 character (e.g. an accented name) lands short of the real terminator, so the frame never completes and the caller times out waiting for a reply that already arrived.

The deployment-local bridge refuses to serve a queue wire binding whose legacyBindingContentHash does not match the reviewed LegacyCapabilityBinding it was handed — the coherence property that stops a bridge from silently serving an unreviewed or since-changed candidate. Delete the check and any wire binding is accepted for any binding, hash mismatch or not.

A repeated idempotency key must return the identical cached reply without re-executing the business side — what makes an outer bounded retry safe at all. Delete the cache check and every call re-executes the handler, so a retried call can observe a different outcome than the one that actually happened.

Every exchange the double receives increments its attempt counter, which is the only way a caller can prove the bridge made exactly one broker attempt per HTTP call and never retried internally. Delete the increment and a silent internal retry loop would be unobservable.

The reviewed timeout is enforced by racing the broker call against a timer — the one place a hung exchange is ever turned into a failure. Delete the race and a broker that never replies leaves the call pending forever instead of failing closed.

A broker timeout must answer with a structured, non-retryable upstream_timeout — never a hang and never a false success. Delete the branch and a timeout falls through to the generic transport-failure response, losing the distinction the runtime's own status-code mapping (packages/runtime/src/errors.ts) depends on.

A binding may be promoted to conformance_passed only from not_implemented — never a second time, and never from a status this function does not recognize. Delete the guard and an already-promoted binding could be silently re-promoted, an operation with no equivalent to a lower-safety direction.
expectedCredentials surfaces mtls client-certificate material by its declared reference NAMES only, in an auth_required error a stranded caller reads -- never the resolved PEM value.

A resolved custom_header credential is carried verbatim under its declared carrier (a vendor's own header name and optional scheme prefix) -- never collapsed to a generic Authorization: Bearer header the way every OAuth/JWT variant is.

oauth2_authorization_code auth always compiles review_required, never approved by a manifest state override, however complete its PKCE/token mechanics are -- end-user authority is a human decision, not a material-completeness one.
A named principal missing a scope an operation's auth.scopes requires is refused before any upstream call -- never silently allowed through because the check was skipped.
A rate-limited or budget-exhausted refusal is never marked retryable -- a caller (SDK, agent, CLI) that respects the envelope must not loop hammering a budget that is already exhausted.

A bare `conflict` error code alone is not evidence of an idempotency-replay contradiction -- an ordinary business conflict (e.g. "this resource already exists") returns the same code and can itself be perfectly idempotent to repeat. Only a record carrying the runtime idempotency ledger's own "replay" evidence (SpooledRecord.ledger) proves the runtime treated it as a repeat of a specific earlier call. Drop the ledger check and any recorded conflict on a naturally-idempotent operation opens a high-severity case, alarm-fatiguing an operator over routine business conflicts.

The drift alarm routes an idempotency-replay contradiction through the EXISTING contested_safety_semantic deficiency (classify-idempotency's registered trigger) -- never a made-up code -- so opening a case actually reaches a real, evidence-compatible skill instead of silently finding nothing to open.

A manifest's state: approved on an oauth2_authorization_code operation is only granted when BOTH reviewed_by and review_reason are non-empty -- deleting the reviewer/reason guard would let a bare `state: approved`, with neither field named, compile straight to approved with no one on record for delegating the end user's authority.

SecretManagerCredentialResolver -- the DEFAULT outbound resolver when ANVIL_CREDENTIALS is unset -- delegates mtls, custom_header, and oauth2_authorization_code to the wrapped EnvCredentialResolver instead of hard-failing them, so an approved, certified operation using one of these three schemes actually resolves credentials on a default-configured deploy instead of failing auth_required on every call (Codex review, PR #43, finding 1).

`anvil auth login` builds redirect_uri from the provider's DECLARED loopback host (127.0.0.1 or localhost, exactly as registered) with only the port substituted, on both the authorize request and the token exchange -- an OAuth server compares redirect_uri byte-for-byte, so silently rewriting a registered `localhost` host to `127.0.0.1` would make a correctly-configured client reject the flow (Codex review, PR #43, finding 2).

When a principal directory IS configured for this session but the caller's own credential did not resolve to an entry in it, execute() refuses fail-closed rather than silently falling back to the anonymous, every-scope principal -- deleting this gate would let a misconfigured/mistyped/unmatched credential grant every scope.

From two bundles on, --fleet namespaces each bundle's authProfile by its own stable id before credentialProfileName adds the security-scheme suffix -- deleting the per-bundle namespace would let two bundles whose schemes share a name (both "oauth", say) resolve the SAME ANVIL_<PROFILE>_* variables, so one service's credential could be sent to another's origin.

A bundle is ready only when its certification is BOTH status:"passed" AND its hash still matches the bundle's CURRENT content (fresh) -- deleting the freshness half would let a stale, copied, or mismatched certification.json (a compiler-owned file edited after `anvil certify` ran) still report ready:true.

The SDK plan carries the token endpoint's DECLARED client authentication method, so every generated client refreshes the way the runtime does for the same contract -- collapsing it to the default would send HTTP Basic to a provider registered for client_secret_post, which rejects it outright, while every env-var name the manifest promises still matches.

Auth drift fails a bundle whose generated source lost the declared token-endpoint client auth -- without this check a language could quietly refresh a different way than the CLI and the MCP server while still naming every declared env var, which is the drift this gate exists to catch.

An exported-but-blank credential env var is NO credential, exactly as the runtime resolver reads it -- treating the empty string as a real token makes the client send an empty bearer instead of falling through to the refresh the contract declares, which is what a .env file or an unpopulated CI secret leaves behind.

An authorization-code contract cannot declare private_key_jwt client authentication: neither the runtime's refresh nor any of the four SDK helpers mints an RFC 7523 assertion, so declaring it would promise what no surface keeps and every one of them would fall back to sending a client secret a private-key client does not have. Scoped to this scheme -- the client-credentials and token-exchange resolvers DO implement the method.

The authorization-code refresh fails closed for private_key_jwt rather than sending a client_secret grant -- without this the serving path would hand a private-key client's secret-post form to a provider that expects a signed assertion, which is both wrong on the wire and a credential the client never declared.

client_auth is LAST in the Python refresh helper's signature so a caller written against an earlier generation keeps its meaning -- inserting it before expiry_skew_seconds silently rebinds a positional 60.0 into the client-auth slot, selecting the post branch and sending client_id where Basic was intended.
mutants.find:
client_secret: Optional[str] = None,
    expiry_skew_seconds: float = 30.0,
    opener: Any = None,
    client_auth: str = "client_secret_basic",
mutants.replace:
client_secret: Optional[str] = None,
    client_auth: str = "client_secret_basic",
    expiry_skew_seconds: float = 30.0,
    opener: Any = None,

mutants.control: A disambiguation must leave every rewritten member carrying a content word its siblings do not all carry. Remove the check and a reword whose every word the siblings could say just as truthfully — a rewrite that cannot change which tool a router picks — is passed on to a reviewer as a fix.

A `disambiguate` patch rewrites what several served tools SAY at once, so it is pinned to the review tier on the FIELD like the other two group keys. Drop it from the guard and a harness can reword K tools' served text with no person in the loop.
mutants.find: if ("workflow" in set || "capability" in set || "disambiguate" in set) {

mutants.control: Every arm of the group proposal union goes through the benchmark-scored admission, keyed off GROUP_PATCH_KEYS so a new arm cannot reach a reviewer unmeasured by simply not being named. Narrow it back to the two composition keys and a disambiguation lands with no delta at all — no refusal for a rewrite that makes routing worse, and no numbers for the reviewer.

A disambiguation applies to every named member or to none. Remove the guard and an unresolvable reference leaves a half-disambiguated catalog — some members moved apart, the rest still colliding — which is not the change the receipt approved.
mutants.replace: // mutant: apply what resolves, skip what does not

mutants.control: A behaviour-check token no vocabulary defines cannot be decided, so it is reported ungraded. Make it pass instead and the runner launders an unrunnable check into a green report — which is the exact defect the runner was built to remove, reproduced one level up.
The pass rate counts ungraded expectations in its denominator. Drop them and the rate RISES as more undecidable checks are added — a score that improves by measuring less.

Every concept token the emitters write is defined here, and the drift gate holds that equal in both directions. Remove a definition and a shipped behaviour check goes back to naming a word nothing defines — the state that made these files unrunnable for years.

The route table the prebuilt runtime reads at boot is written beside it as webhooks.json. Drop it and every compiled bundle boots a server that refuses to start (it fails closed on the missing artifact) — or, if that refusal were ever weakened, a server serving an empty route table under a hash that says otherwise.

Every bundle records which @anvil/mcp-runtime built its server and the sha256 of the exact bytes (runtime.lock.json). Drop it and a bundle's runtime provenance goes back to being implicit — inferable only from whichever Anvil happened to compile it.

Return an empty document instead and a partial or tampered copy serves silently — with no route table, or no catalog — under a self-hash that no longer matches what was certified. Every request, GET included, must carry a Host of 127.0.0.1:<port> or localhost:<port>. Delete the check and a page whose domain was re-pointed at 127.0.0.1 (DNS rebinding) is same-origin with the socket, so it reads the API and the page that embeds the token with a plain fetch, no token or foreign Origin needed.

With inbound auth unset the fleet listener answers only a loopback Host on the port the connection arrived on, on every route. Delete the check and a DNS-rebinding page can POST to /mcp or /call/* same-origin and drive the fleet's tools as the anonymous principal.

The stdio fleet's unauthenticated /readyz (bundle ids, tool counts, certification hashes) listens on 127.0.0.1 unless ANVIL_FLEET_READYZ_HOST names an address. Widen the default and every interface on the host serves it.

The stdio fleet keeps its bundle clients and /readyz until the session ends (transport close, stdin end, SIGTERM/SIGINT), not until McpServer.connect resolves. Resolve early and every tools/call answers "Not connected".
A /readyz bind failure (EADDRINUSE, EADDRNOTAVAIL) is one stderr line and the MCP session keeps running, instead of an unhandled 'error' event crashing the fleet.

On a loopback bind the stdio fleet's unauthenticated /readyz answers only a loopback Host on its own port. Delete the check and a DNS-rebinding page reads every bundle id, tool count and certification hash.

With inbound auth unset the HTTP fleet answers a request carrying an Origin header only when it is its own loopback origin (MCP Streamable HTTP: a present, invalid Origin is a 403). Delete the check and a page on another origin can drive the fleet's tools.

Bound to loopback, the facade answers only a Host naming a loopback address with its own port. Delete the check and a DNS-rebinding page reaches it as its own origin, reading /readyz and any reply without an Origin header to refuse.

The facade's Host gate requires the port the request reached, not just a loopback name, so a page served from another local port (or a forward to a different port) is not treated as the bridge's own address.

parseRequestTarget turns a request target the URL parser refuses (`GET //`, `GET http://[`, which Node's HTTP parser accepts) into `undefined` for the listener to answer 400. Let it throw and every async listener that parses req.url is one `curl http://host//` from an unhandled rejection that ends the process.

createGuardedServer answers a listener that rejects (500, or a destroyed socket once a response has started) instead of leaving the rejection unhandled. Delete the catch and any throw a route fails to anticipate ends runtime/server.js, mcp/server-sse.js, or the fleet listener.

A listener that throws before its first await (or a non-async one) is caught too: the call runs inside the Promise executor, so a synchronous throw becomes a rejection the guard answers rather than an uncaught exception in the 'request' event.

Once a response has started, a failure destroys the socket so a client never mistakes a half-written body for a whole one. Without the headersSent branch the guard writes a second status line, which throws inside the catch handler and leaves the connection hanging.
The guard's 500 is a fixed envelope; the error's own text (which can carry a path, a vault location, or a provider's state) never reaches the caller.
A reporter that throws cannot turn the guard's own catch handler into the unhandled rejection it exists to prevent.

A HAR entry whose request.url will not parse is reported with the URL cut at its query, and not shown at all when that part has an "@" (a malformed URL's userinfo can't be located reliably). Show the raw string and a user:pass or api_key carried in that URL is written into the compiled AIR's diagnostics.

A HAR request.url with an opaque origin (data:, blob:, or user:pass@host/... read as scheme "user") is skipped with a warning. Lower it and the server is the string "null" and the whole rest of the URL, credential included, becomes an operation path.

A server base written as https://user:pass@host, in any spelling, is lowered to scheme, host and port only. Drop the strip and every base with userinfo is refused, so a request URL with a credential in it loses its real host to the placeholder.

An oauth2 authUrl or accessTokenUrl is lowered without userinfo or a query value whose name marks it as a credential. Copy the query verbatim and that credential is written into the lowered security scheme and from there into AIR's token endpoint.

A URL the parser accepts with userinfo (https:/user:pass@host, with one slash) is rebuilt from its parsed parts. Return it unchanged whenever no query parameter has to go, and that userinfo is copied into a lowered oauth2 scheme.

mutants.control: A raw Postman URL reads any run of slashes or backslashes after https: as "//", as browsers do. Without it https:/user:pass@host/x parses with "https:" as the host and the credential becomes part of an operation path.
xsd:time lowers to a pattern whose timezone is optional, as XSD defines it. Make the timezone required and the served tool refuses "10:00:00", a valid XSD time.

The xsd:time pattern keeps XSD's ranges: hours to 23 or 24:00:00, minutes and seconds to 59, offsets to 14:00. Loosen it to bare two-digit fields and 99:99:99Z or +99:99 pass the served tool's validation and fail at the SOAP service.
